Communication accessibility

Project Overview

American Sign Language is an important communication method for Deaf and hard-of-hearing communities, but communication barriers can arise when an ASL user interacts with someone who does not understand sign language. This project investigates how ordinary consumer hardware and local machine-learning software can help convert visible signs into information that a non-signer can read or hear.

The completed prototype uses a Logitech C920 webcam secured to a chest mount harness and connected to a laptop by USB. The laptop performs video capture, landmark detection, gesture recognition, verification, sentence generation, text display, and speech output locally. The system is a proof-of-concept for selected dynamic ASL words; it is not intended to replace an interpreter or serve as a complete ASL translation system.

Primary Objective

Recognize selected dynamic ASL words in real time and convert verified results into natural English text and offline speech output.

Hardware Platform

Logitech C920 RGB webcam, chest mount harness, USB connection, and a laptop used as the local processing platform.

Operating Conditions

One signer, adequate indoor lighting, a stable camera position, and both hands visible whenever a two-handed sign is performed.

Design choice: A standard RGB webcam was selected instead of sensor gloves or a depth camera because it offers a stronger balance of portability, accessibility, computational efficiency, and cost without requiring specialized wearable electronics.

End-to-end recognition pipeline

System Design

The design follows a modular pipeline so that capture, recognition, verification, language processing, and output can be developed and tested independently. All software modules are implemented in Python and run locally on the laptop.

1. Video Capture

The chest-mounted Logitech C920 captures the signing space from a stable forward-facing position.

2. Hand Landmarks

MediaPipe extracts 21 landmarks per hand. Coordinates are normalized to reduce differences caused by hand size, position, and camera distance.

3. GRU Recognition

Each frame contains 90 features from both hands. Sequences of 50 frames are processed by a GRU neural network to classify dynamic ASL words.

4. Result Verification

Pose, direction, and motion checks compare a prediction with word-specific templates and thresholds, reducing false detections from similar or unintended movements.

5. Sentence Generation

A lightweight Qwen language model reorganizes verified word sequences into more natural English while being instructed not to add new meaning.

6. Accessible Output

The generated sentence is displayed in the laptop interface and spoken using an offline text-to-speech engine.

Final acceptance rule: A predicted word is accepted only when the GRU confidence reaches its threshold and every required pose, direction, and motion check passes. Otherwise, the system returns Unknown.

Controlled demonstration

Results & Testing

The completed prototype captured live video from the chest-mounted webcam, detected hand landmarks, buffered fixed-length sequences, recognized supported words, verified predictions, and produced text and speech output. The report documents successful controlled demonstrations of words including Hello, Coffee, I, and Want.

31

Dynamic ASL Words

A selected vocabulary was used to demonstrate real-time word recognition.

622

Training Samples

Word-specific pose, direction, and motion templates were produced from the collected dataset.

$110

Added Hardware Cost

Estimated direct cost in CAD for the webcam, chest mount, and cable or accessories, excluding the existing laptop and labour.

Validated Functions

Webcam capture, mount stability, MediaPipe tracking, sequence buffering, GRU recognition, verification, text display, and speech output all passed their documented subsystem tests.

Current Limitations

Performance can decline under poor lighting, hand occlusion, complex backgrounds, camera-position changes, or signing styles not represented in the training data.

Recommended Next Steps

Expand the vocabulary and user diversity, add continuous-sign and facial-expression analysis, improve the interface, and investigate deployment on mobile hardware.

Scope statement: Testing confirms the project’s main functional objectives under controlled conditions. Additional multi-user validation is required before the system could be considered for practical communication scenarios.
